scams.name: The Krakow Old Town 'Pretty Girl' Strip Club Bill
scams.description:
They are friendly, laughing, and within two minutes one of them mentions a 'fun club' she knows just two streets away — locals only, much better than the tourist places, no queue. She gestures down a side street near St. Mary's. Your group hesitates for half a second, but the women are already walking, and the social momentum carries you along. The 'club' is a discreet door behind a curtain on a quiet street with no signage, no menu visible from outside, and a bouncer who waves you in.

Inside, the lighting is low, two more women are already at a table, and the bartender pours bottles of champagne before anyone has ordered. The bill, when it arrives ninety minutes later, is PLN 8,000–20,000 (€1,800–4,500), with no menu reference and an itemization that lists drinks at €100 a glass and 'private dance' surcharges that no one explained. When your group refuses to pay, three bouncers appear at the door, the women have vanished, and the bartender calmly suggests the ATM around the corner.

The Krakow strip-club honey-trap is the city's single most documented and financially damaging tourist scam. The U.S. Embassy in Warsaw, the U.K. Foreign Office, and Kraków city police have all issued formal warnings going back more than a decade. r/poland and the Krakow TripAdvisor forum carry first-person accounts running from €500 to €5,000+ per group, and several documented cases involve drugged drinks (often gamma-hydroxybutyrate) and forced multi-hour ATM withdrawal runs under bouncer escort.

The pattern is consistent — attractive English-speaking women near the Rynek who 'just happen' to suggest a specific bar, an unmarked venue down a side street, no menu prices, drinks brought before ordering, bouncers at the door — and the venues themselves rotate frequently to stay ahead of police. Krakow city police have been known to escort groups to ATMs to recover funds, but only when the scam is reported in real time and the group can identify the venue afterward.

Never follow strangers, especially attractive women who approach unprompted, to any bar in Krakow's Old Town — pick your own venue, ideally an established place like Singer Café, Mleczarnia, or Alchemia in Kazimierz where prices are visible and management is reputable. If you find yourself at a venue with no menu in sight or drinks arriving before you ordered, leave immediately. If you are handed a fraudulent bill, refuse to pay, demand the police be called (dial 997 — the bar bluffs about police; police actually side with victims), and stay calm. Save the U.S. Embassy Warsaw line on your phone (+48 22 504 2000) and never withdraw cash under bouncer pressure.
scams.avoidance: Never follow strangers to clubs in Old Town Only go to venues you researched beforehand Use Booking.com/Google Maps to find reputable bars If you end up somewhere sketchy, leave before ordering
scams.location: Old Town (Stare Miasto), around Main Market Square
scams.tldr: You and two friends from your hostel are wandering past the Cloth Hall on Rynek Główny at midnight, three beers in, when two attractive young women fall into step beside you and ask in fluent English if you know any good places to keep the night going.

scams.name: The Krakow Kantor '0% Commission' Rate Trap
scams.description:
The teller behind the glass takes your two €100 notes, taps a calculator, and slides PLN 700 across the counter. You count the bills, thank her, and walk out. It feels like a clean transaction. Back at your hotel, you check the actual EUR-to-PLN rate on the National Bank of Poland (NBP) website — €200 should have given you about PLN 870 at the interbank rate. You have just lost roughly PLN 170 (€38) on a single exchange.

The '0% commission' sign was technically true: there was no separate commission charge. The fraud lives in the spread between the kantor's posted exchange rate and the interbank rate, and that rate is displayed in tiny font on a back wall while the '0% COMMISSION' sign dominates the window. Tourist-area kantors around Rynek Główny routinely offer rates 10–20% worse than NBP's published mid-rate, sometimes worse. The few honest kantors in the Old Town display rates clearly on a digital board outside; the predatory ones hide them.

A second variation runs at the ATM. Polish ATMs, especially in tourist areas and hotel lobbies, present a Dynamic Currency Conversion screen asking whether you want to be charged in your home currency or in PLN. The home-currency option uses a deliberately poor exchange rate (5–15% worse than your bank's rate) and is presented as 'helpful.' Choosing PLN — and letting your home bank handle the conversion — is almost always the better deal. The pattern is the same as Budapest's Euronet ATMs and applies at Polish bank-branded ATMs too.

The kantor and DCC scams are well-documented across r/poland, the Krakow TripAdvisor forum, and the National Bank of Poland's own consumer-protection materials. The reliable kantors in central Krakow (Kantor SuperSam at Rynek Główny 9, Kantor Plus on Karmelicka, Kantor Studio on Karmelicka) display clear rates outside, post both buy and sell rates digitally, and stay within 1–2% of the NBP rate. Anything advertising 'no commission' without showing the rate prominently is the warning sign.

Always check the NBP rate (nbp.pl) on your phone before exchanging money in Krakow — anything more than 2% off the mid-rate is a bad deal. Use only kantors that display both buy and sell rates clearly outside on a digital board, ignore any '0% commission' sign that does not also show the rate, and avoid kantors directly on Rynek Główny in favor of a few streets away (Karmelicka, Sławkowska). At every ATM and card terminal, decline DCC and choose to be charged in PLN. Use Revolut or Wise for most cash needs — both offer real-rate conversion with minimal fees and work seamlessly at Polish ATMs.
scams.avoidance: Always decline DCC at ATMs — choose to pay in Polish zloty Use Revolut or Wise for cash exchange If using a kantor, check rates at NBP.pl first Avoid exchange booths right next to tourist attractions
scams.tldr: A small currency-exchange booth (kantor) two doors down from the Cloth Hall has a bright '0% COMMISSION' sign in the window, which seems straightforward, and you step inside to convert €200 into Polish złoty for the day's expenses.

scams.name: The Main Market Square Horse-Carriage Per-Person Reveal
scams.description:
It seems fair. You and your partner climb in, the driver shakes the reins, and you spend twenty-five minutes clopping past the Cloth Hall, down Grodzka Street to Wawel Castle, and back up Floriańska to the rank. The light is good, you take photos, you tip the horse with a carrot the driver hands you. You feel good about the choice. He pulls up at the rank, helps you down, and presents the bill: PLN 600.

When you object, he points calmly at a small laminated card on the inside of the carriage door that you never saw. The PLN 150 quote, he explains, was per person. There are two of you, so PLN 300. There is a 'per-stop' surcharge of PLN 100 for each of the two photo stops. There is a PLN 100 'evening rate' because you got in after 4 p.m. The total is PLN 600 (€135). The original PLN 150 has nearly quadrupled, and the price reveal happens at the end when refusing means a public scene at the busiest tourist square in Poland.

The horse-carriage per-person reveal is one of Krakow's most consistent medium-grade scams, documented on r/poland, the Krakow TripAdvisor forum, and most updated guidebooks. The Krakow city council has tried to standardize carriage pricing — the official posted rate is roughly PLN 250–350 for a thirty-minute ride for up to four passengers — but enforcement is weak and individual drivers operate freelance, with the 'per-person,' 'per-stop,' and 'evening rate' add-ons calibrated to the moment you cannot easily walk away.

A second variation involves the route. Some drivers shorten the agreed itinerary by skipping Wawel or cutting the Castle loop, then claim the price was for a shorter ride than agreed and demand more for the 'extended' version. Others stop at a 'recommended' shop or restaurant where they collect commission. The horse-related variations are also worth knowing about — animal welfare in Krakow's carriage industry is contested, and some travelers boycott on principle even when pricing is fair.

Lock the price in writing before any horse carriage moves on Rynek Główny — ask the exact phrase: 'What is the TOTAL price for the full ride back to this same spot, for [number] passengers, with no add-ons?' and have the driver write it on a piece of paper or send it to your phone. The official posted rate is roughly PLN 250–350 for thirty minutes for up to four passengers. Refuse any 'per-person' framing or 'per-stop' surcharge, and walk away if the driver will not show you the rate card. If a driver demands inflated payment, photograph the carriage number, refuse the disputed amount, and call the Krakow Tourist Police at +48 12 615 7311 or dial 997.
scams.avoidance: Confirm the TOTAL price in writing before you get in Ask if it's per person or for the whole carriage Walk away if they won't show you a price list Book through an official tourism office instead
scams.tldr: A horse-drawn carriage at the rank on Rynek Główny looks like the perfect way to round out an afternoon — red velvet seats, a uniformed driver, the spires of St. Mary's behind it — and the driver quotes you PLN 150 for a 'standard tour' of the Old Town and Wawel.

scams.name: The Krakow John Paul II Airport Taxi Tout
scams.description:
You name a hotel near Rynek Główny. He nods, says 'PLN 200, very good price, follow me,' and walks you past the official iCar Taxi rank toward an unmarked silver sedan parked near the curb. The car has a roof sign that looks vaguely taxi-like but no company branding. He loads your bag into the trunk, you climb in, and he pulls onto Medweckiego.

The legitimate metered fare from KRK to the Old Town runs PLN 60–90 (€14–20) on a posted Kraków Taxi tariff. The PLN 200 you just agreed to is more than double the going rate, and some touts will quote €30–50 to outright foreign tourists who do not yet know the currency. The 'meter,' if there is one, runs at three or four times the standard speed and produces a final bill in the PLN 250–350 range. There is no receipt, no recourse, and the driver vanishes once you reach the hotel.

Kraków Police and the airport authority have run periodic enforcement against unlicensed taxi touts at KRK, but the pattern persists because the official taxi rank is two minutes' walk past the curb where the touts intercept arriving passengers, and most travelers do not know to look further. The legitimate Kraków taxis are clearly branded — iCar, Wawel Taxi, Mega Taxi, Radio Taxi 919, all with company logos, posted tariff cards, and printed receipts.

The cleanest fix is to skip every curbside conversation. Bolt is the dominant rideshare in Poland, runs on the airport Wi-Fi, shows the fare upfront in the app at PLN 70–100 to the Old Town, and takes about 20 minutes. Uber operates in Krakow at similar rates. The 100E airport bus does not exist for KRK (Kraków uses Train Line 1 from the airport station to Kraków Główny in 18 minutes for PLN 17), so train + a short walk is also viable. The unofficial 'TAXI'-badge touts are, by definition, not part of any of these systems.

Book Bolt or Uber on the airport Wi-Fi before walking outside — the fare to the Old Town is PLN 70–100 fixed in-app, and the driver is rated and tracked. If you prefer a licensed taxi, walk past the curb to the official taxi rank, use only branded iCar or Wawel Taxi cars, and confirm the meter is on with the standard PLN 8 base before the car moves. The fastest budget option is Train Line 1 — KRK to Kraków Główny in 18 minutes for PLN 17, runs every 30 minutes. Ignore any 'taxi' offer made inside the terminal or at the curb by a person without company branding; report aggressive touts to airport security.
scams.avoidance: Pre-book a taxi via iCar or Bolt from the airport app Use the official MDA (Municipal Transport Authority) taxi stand inside the terminal Agree on price before getting in if you use a street taxi Bolt and Uber are reliable and cheaper
scams.tldr: You walk out of the arrivals hall at Kraków John Paul II Airport with a single bag, and a man in a black jacket with a small 'TAXI' badge approaches you immediately, smiles, and asks where you are going.

scams.name: The Krakow Old Town 'Free Shot' Bar Promoter
scams.description:
The pitch is light. He says it is a popular local place with cheap drinks, that the free shot is no obligation, and that you can leave any time. Your group is already six beers in and looking for the next stop. You shrug and follow him into a basement bar with low ceilings, no menu visible from the entrance, and a bartender who hands you all small shots of clear vodka before anyone has ordered. The first drink really is free.

The bartender then suggests a 'house cocktail' — neon blue, served in a tall glass with sparklers — and brings four of them to your table without explicitly asking. The drinks keep coming. Around midnight someone in your group asks for the bill. The total is PLN 800–2,000 (€180–450), with cocktails listed at PLN 80–120 each (roughly four times the going Krakow rate) and several drinks no one remembers ordering. There is no menu. The promoter has vanished.

The 'free shot' bar is a softer cousin of the strip-club honey-trap from scam #1, and it works on the same principle: a friendly opener that puts you in a venue with no transparent pricing, then a slow drip of unsolicited drinks at inflated rates. The U.S. Embassy in Warsaw and the U.K. Foreign Office both flag the pattern in their Krakow advisories, and r/poland carries first-person accounts going back years. The venues themselves rotate — a bar that runs the scam in October may be under different management by spring — but the choreography is consistent across the Old Town nightclub strip.

A second variation involves the 'cocktail tour' that promoters sell as a package deal: PLN 100 for entry to four bars and a free shot at each. The tour is real but the participating bars are selected for their tolerance of the upsell pattern, and the shots are calibrated to lower judgment ahead of the inflated cocktail menu. Reputable Krakow nightlife — Singer Café, Mleczarnia, Alchemia in Kazimierz, or any bar with prices clearly listed inside — does not run free-shot promoter campaigns at all.

Never accept a 'free shot' or 'welcome drink' offer from a promoter on Floriańska, Szewska, or near Rynek Główny — the free drink is the hook for an inflated tab. Ignore promoter flyers entirely, look up specific bars on Google Maps before going in, and only enter venues with a printed menu visible from the entrance and recent reviews mentioning consistent pricing. Pay for each drink as it is served rather than running a tab, and refuse any cocktail you did not explicitly order. Reputable Krakow nightlife exists in Kazimierz (Alchemia, Singer Café, Mleczarnia) — go there instead.
scams.avoidance: Never accept 'free' drinks from strangers outside clubs Look up bar reviews before going in Always ask for a menu and confirm prices before ordering Stick to reputable venues recommended by your hostel
scams.tldr: A friendly young promoter on Floriańska Street steps in front of you with a stack of flyers, smiles, and offers you a free shot of vodka and a 'welcome drink' if you and your group come inside the bar he is repping for the night.

scams.name: The Main Market Square Fake-Charity Petition
scams.description:
The vest looks vaguely official. The clipboard has a printed form with a small charity logo, several signatures already on it, and what looks like a name-and-address column for donations. She holds out a pen, says her English is limited, and points at where you should sign. Two friends of hers drift over from the side and a third stands a step behind you, smiling, holding her own clipboard. The encounter feels coordinated but harmless.

You sign. She immediately points to the donation column and asks for €10–20 in 'support' for the cause. While you are reaching for your wallet, the second woman who drifted over is now standing very close on your other side, leaning in to read what you wrote, and the third person behind you is closer than necessary. The clipboard is held at chest level, blocking your view of your own hands.

The fake-charity petition is two scams running simultaneously. The first is the cash donation itself — the charity does not exist, the signatures on the clipboard are fake, and the orange vest is bought online. The second is pickpocketing: while you are focused on the clipboard and the pen, the people standing too close on either side are working your pockets and bag, and the clipboard itself is positioned to block your peripheral vision. Some operators run only the first scam, some only the second, and many run both.

The pattern is documented across r/poland, the Krakow tourist police's own advisory pages, and matches identical scams in Paris near the Eiffel Tower, in Rome near the Colosseum, and in Barcelona on La Rambla. The 'deaf and mute' framing is a common variant, designed to discourage tourists from speaking up because the operator pretends not to be able to communicate. Real charities in Poland do not solicit cash donations from foreign tourists on the street, and any legitimate petition would not require a payment to sign.

Walk past anyone who approaches you with a clipboard at Rynek Główny, near St. Mary's, or at the train station — there is no legitimate version of the interaction in these locations. Do not stop, do not engage, do not slow down. If someone steps directly into your path, change direction without breaking stride and say 'nie dziękuję' (no thank you) firmly. Keep your wallet in a front pocket and your bag zipped and worn across your front; people standing close while you are distracted are looking for it. Real charities do not solicit cash from tourists in tourist squares.
scams.avoidance: Just walk away — you're not obligated to interact Keep your hand on your wallet if anyone approaches in a group Legitimate charities don't solicit in tourist areas this way Say 'nie dziękuję' (no thank you) firmly
scams.location: Main Market Square, Wawel Castle area
scams.tldr: You are walking across Rynek Główny on a sunny afternoon when a young woman with a clipboard and an orange high-visibility vest steps into your path with a warm smile, gestures at her clipboard, and asks if you will sign a petition for deaf children.
